subtopic: CIVIL DEFENCE OFFICERS
CIVIL DEFENCE OFFICERS
speechtext:
1.	Is there an officer in any department of the federal government primarily responsible for civil defence?
2.	Who is responsible in each of the Canadian provinces and in the Northwest and Yukon Territories?

3.	Is there a federal commissioner of civil defence and, if so, in what manner is his office organized and how does it operate?
4.	Among the Canadian armed forces, are there any specialized units for civil defence operations?
5.	Has the government had any fairly recent talks on the subject of civil defence with the provincial attorneys general or representatives of the premiers of the provinces?
6.	How many emergency centres and underground stations has the government built in (a) each province (b) what were the costs involved (c) who will be in charge of such stations?

subtopic: CIVIL DEFENCE OFFICERS
speechtext:
1. The director of the federal emergency measures organization is responsible for co-ordinating the emergency planning activities of all federal departments and agencies, and providing assistance and guidance to provincial authorities.
2.	Each province has appointed an officer who is in charge of the emergency planning activities in that province. Similarly, in the Yukon and Northwest Territories, the territorial authorities have designated emergency measures co-ordinators. The federal E.M.O. also has officers in each provincial capital to co-ordinate federal emergency planning activities with the plans developed by provincial authorities.
3.	There is no official with the formal title of federal commissioner of civil defence. As has already been stated, the co-ordination of civil emergency planning at the federal level is the responsibility of the director of the emergency measures organization. Pursuant to order in council 1963-993 the organization has the status of a department of government. The Minister of Industry is the responsible minister. The organization is comprised of a headquarters staff in Ottawa, a civil defence college at Arnprior, and offices in each provincial capital.
4.	All units both regular and militia undergo training in national survival and rescue work. At army headquarters there is a senior officer (major-general survival) with a staff, who is responsible for developing policy and plans for the Canadian army's role in survival operations and for the co-ordination of such matters with other government departments.
5.	The last meeting with provincial ministers responsible for civil emergency planning was held in Ottawa on December 3, 1962, at which time all provinces were represented.
6.	(a) A major emergency operating centre has been built in each of the following provinces: British Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec and Nova Scotia. In addition there is a complex of emergency facilities in the vicinity of Ottawa, (b) $55,610,000 including land, buildings, and equipment, (c) The emergency measures organization has been charged with the responsibility for developing these operating centres under arrangements with the army whereby the latter

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. Question No. 5 standing on the order paper in my name is dated February 18. It relates to information which I endeavoured to obtain from the government regarding the construction of the federal penal institution at Springhill, Nova Scotia. I have in my hand a release appearing in the Halifax Chronic le-Herald of April 1, 1964 which reads as follows:
Inquiries of the Ministry
Tenders on construction of the new young offenders institution at Springhill will be called by mid-April and the federal government expects to award the contract by the end of April, for a construction start early in May, labour minister MacEachen said Tuesday.
Mr. MacEachen, Nova Scotia's representative in the federal cabinet, also told the Chronicle-Herald that a $254,590 contract for provision of high temperature water generators and auxiliary equipment at the institution had been awarded to Dominion Bridge Company of Montreal.
The content of that press release, Mr. Speaker, is the information I seek in my question which is on the order paper. Yet the government has been willing to provide the information to the Minister of Labour and to disregard my rights as a member of this house.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: MR. RICARD    REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Is he in a position to give a report regarding the incident that took place yesterday in Cyprus in which members of the Canadian contingent of the United Nations force was involved? At the same time, is he now in a position to give the house further information regarding the directives to the force and the circumstances under which the force may act when its freedom is interfered with?

Inquiries of the Ministry

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: MR. RICARD    REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with regard to the last part of the question, the position is no different from what it was last week, when I said that it was not in the interests of the force and of the assignment given to the force to give the directives. This was the position taken yesterday in the British House of Commons by Mr. Sandys when he indicated that the matter was one that rested with the secretary general and pointed out, as I pointed out last week, that directives to armed forces as such are never given out by any authority. Mr. Sandys said:
Since recent incidents have caused some anxiety I think it right to inform the house that we are satisfied that the directions under which the United Nations troops have been operating give them adequate authority to use such force as may be absolutely necessary for self defence and to enable them to discharge their mission. The secretary general has assured us that he recognizes that the force must have the powers necessary to fulfil its task.
With regard to the first part of the right hon. member's question, General Gyani who is in charge of the force has made representations respecting this matter to the government of Cyprus.

maintopic: MR. RICARD    REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: What attitude has the Canadian government taken and what representations has it made regarding Canadians being interfered with as they were?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: MR. RICARD    REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
I may say to my
right hon. friend that Canada is not holding itself aloof from developments which could have a bearing on the outcome of the problem in Cyprus. We have a high commissioner accredited to the government of Cyprus and he is in continuous contact with the Cypriot authorities. Our permanent mission to the United Nations is similarly in constant contact with the secretary general and the United Nations officials directing the United Nations peace keeping operation. We are availing ourselves of these proper channels for the expression of our views on such matters as freedom of movement for the United Nations force which was guaranteed by the Cypriot government in the status of forces agreement. I tabled yesterday copies of that agreement which clearly is not yet fully effective.
I might say that the Canadian and British forces in Cyprus deserve the highest commendation for the restraint they have shown in the trying circumstances which have arisen when freedom of movement has been temporarily denied to them. I am satisfied that the operations of the peace keeping force have reduced considerably the very great potential danger which existed on that island a few weeks ago and which has not completely disappeared.

maintopic: MR. RICARD    REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: After all that verbiage will the minister now answer the question? Has the Canadian government made a protest with regard to the interference by Cypriots with that portion of the Canadian force that was interfered with yesterday?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: MR. RICARD    REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sorry that my method of response does not satisfy the right hon. gentleman. It is not my fault if I do not possess his great capacity for lucid expression, but I cannot add anything to what I have said.

maintopic: MR. RICARD    REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Loose expression.

maintopic: MR. RICARD    REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the Secretary of State for External Affairs undertake to request the secretary general of the United Nations to release and publish the directives that were given to the troops, inasmuch as it is reported in the Globe and Mail this morning that in the parliament of the United Kingdom yesterday Mr. Sandys agreed to do this?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: MR. RICARD    REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the views of Canada with regard to the directives were discussed by me with the secretary general about 10 days ago. With respect to the action taken by Mr. Sandys I can say that there is consultation on this point, but I am convinced from the information available to me now that the course taken by the secretary general in the circumstances is the right course; it is in the interests of fulfilling the assignment for which the international police force was established.
So far as the hon. member's question is concerned, I suggest that he might look at the status of forces agreement tabled yesterday; I think that agreement would perhaps give him some satisfaction.

maintopic: MR. RICARD    REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that the situation in Cyprus has been further complicated by the repudiation by President Makarios of the treaty with Turkey, may I ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs if he himself, directly or through the secretary general, will make representations to Archbishop Makarios to make it perfectly clear that this parliament authorized Canadian forces as part of the United Nations force to maintain peace in Cyprus but not to protect the government of Cyprus against the consequences of its unilateral repudiation of an existing treaty?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: MR. RICARD    REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the British government, the government of Turkey and the government of Greece are parties to the 1960 agreement. I would call my hon. friend's attention to the attitude taken by the British government in this matter; that government would have a treaty qualification to

complain about any act that would involve the abrogation of treaty rights. The course this government must follow, based on the information before us, must be dictated by our view of the effect this will have on the fulfilment of the mission for which the force was established. Our representative in Nicosia is in contact with the government of Cyprus, and with the head of that government, Archbishop Makarios. In my judgment it is not in the public interest for me to say anything further at this time.

maintopic: MR. RICARD    REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
A further supplementary
question, Mr. Speaker. In view of the fact that the foreign minister of Turkey has made it clear that any interference with the small Turkish force in Cyprus will lead to hostilities, I hope that the Secretary of State for External Affairs will make it very clear to the president of Cyprus that Canada would take a very dim view of having Canadian forces caught in a series of hostilities brought about by actions of the government of Cyprus.

maintopic: MR. RICARD    REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend may well be assured that his point of view as expressed now and the point of view of the Canadian government, are not basically different.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speechtext:
Yesterday the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale asked me a question about the initial payment on barley announced by the wheat board two days ago. The average final payment on barley of the 1962 crop was 18.2 cents per bushel compared with 30.2 cents per bushel for the 1961 crop, or 12 cents per bushel lower.
There are two reasons for this decline. First, the carrying charges applicable to the pool account just closed were 4 cents per bushel higher than the carrying charges applicable to the 1961-62 pool account. Second, the average market price realized by the Canadian wheat board for barley sold for the account of the 1962-63 pool was 8 cents

Inquiries of the Ministry per bushel less than the average market price realized lor barley delivered to the 1961-62 pool.
The reason lor the increase in the carrying charges is to be lound in the lact that producer deliveries were considerably higher in 1962-63, at the figure ol 77.6 million bushels, than in 1961-62, with a figure ol 56.4 million bushels, and also because large export sales were made relatively early in the 1961 crop year, whereas a strong demand lor the barley delivered to the 1962-63 pool account did not develop until the fall of 1963.
The reason lor the decreased average market price for barley in the 1962-63 pool was intensified competition for export feed grain markets and a general decline in world feed grain prices.
The hon. member said farmers would be interested in this information as an indication of what they should now be seeding. May I just say that, speaking generally, I am reasonably optimistic about the future with respect to feed grain markets, particularly here in Canada, and I foresee the need for a gradually expanding acreage for the production of barley in the years ahead.

subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO REMARK BY JUSTICE MINISTER
speechtext:
Well, I must say on the point of privilege, that the Secretary of State for External Affairs has suggested to Your Honour and to the committee that I have been misusing the privileges of the house in discussing points of order with Your Honour. All I can say is that no member of the house, in the 11 or so years I have been here, has spent more time discussing points of order, appropriate and otherwise, than the hon. member for Essex East. To suggest that anybody else who deigns to discuss a point of order with Your Honour, or with whomever is sitting in Your Honour's chair, is abusing the rules of the house is a kind of logic that defeats any reasonable person.
While I frankly do not place much stock in the argument I have heard from the Secretary of State for External Affairs and from the minister in charge of the treasury, if Your Honour rules that I cannot discuss this matter of Cyprus, a matter of the greatest importance at the present time, I will obey Your Honour's ruling, but I think it is a very strange and odd attitude on the part of the government.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO REMARK BY JUSTICE MINISTER
speechtext: In my opinion the rules preclude the hon. member from discussing this matter along the lines which he was following a moment ago. If there is some way that any matter can be brought within the ambit and the limitations of vote No. 35e, then of course the Chair would not want to try to restrict the hon. member. But I feel we have a very specific item before us and that our discussion should be limited to this item in the light of the rule of relevancy.

subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO REMARK BY JUSTICE MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to deal specifically with the item before the committee, and in view of the fact that we spent 25 minutes this afternoon on procedure, I shall be very brief because it is my sincere thought that if we are brief and deal with the items in front of us, then perchance we might be able to finish the supplementary estimates by tomorrow night, which I hope we can do.
I would like some information about the Royal Canadian Air Force, and I hope this


will be in order because it concerns something which occurred a number of weeks ago. I regret that the Minister of National Defence is not in his seat. I notice unfortunately he left the chamber just as his supplementary estimates were called, but I hope that the associate minister, or perhaps the Secretary of State for External Affairs, will be able to give the information I seek.
I am sure all members of the committee would appreciate some information as to what was the new arrangement that was worked out a number of weeks ago with France and with NATO relative to the R.C.A.F. The only information we got was that contained in the press several weeks ago, that two of the squadrons are being moved from France to Germany and two are being left in France.
The information received by our defence committee, when we were in France, was to the effect that there were French squadrons in Germany and that they would be kept in Germany because only by having them in Germany could the French squadrons be equipped with nuclear warheads. On what basis are we maintaining two of our squadrons in France when they cannot be equipped there for the purpose for which they were bought by the previous government?
What exactly is the role of the two squadrons now in France, and is it correct that a decision was reached with France and NATO a number of weeks ago that these two squadrons of CF-104 planes are going to have an entirely different role, and will have to be re-adapted or re-equipped to carry conventional warheads in their new role?
On what basis is Canada still maintaining two squadrons in France while France maintains squadrons in Germany? Second, what is their role? Third, because of some mistake, stupidity or misunderstanding by the previous government in its purchase agreements, who has to pay for the re-adaptation of these two CF-104 squadrons in France, and what is the approximate figure of the cost of that readaptation?

subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO REMARK BY JUSTICE MINISTER
speechtext: I do not think I can let pass the reference made by the hon. member for Vancouver East concerning the Minister of National Defence.

subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO REMARK BY JUSTICE MINISTER
speechtext: Well, he did leave just as the item was called.

subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO REMARK BY JUSTICE MINISTER
speechtext: I realize he left, but he did not leave because he did not want to answer questions.

subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO REMARK BY JUSTICE MINISTER
speechtext: I did not say that. I said I noticed he left and I did not comment on the reasons.

subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO REMARK BY JUSTICE MINISTER
speechtext:
Just in case the hon. member might have that somewhere in the back of his mind, I would like to say the minister had to leave the committee, and it was with regret he did so. I would also like to say that I think there has been, on the part of the Minister of National Defence, a very frank and open discourse on what was happening in the Department of National Defence. Also, I believe there will be opportunities within a day or so, in the budget debate, when these matters can be brought up again. Further, as hon. members know, it is understood that all the national defence reorganization may be discussed in the special committee on national defence. It is most unfair if anyone should get the idea on these particular estimates, which are the fifth and last, that we are not willing to give the committee whatever information we can.
The hon. member was asking about the air squadrons in Europe. I do not think the difficult position of the Canadian government in that respect is a secret to anyone, and the purpose of sending the squadrons we had in France to Germany was in order to get out of an impasse which was not of our making. To do this we have given the squadrons remaining in France a reconnaissance role. All our squadrons will have a dual role, both strike and reconnaissance, but the aircraft of the squadrons in France will be limited to the reconnaissance role.
As the hon. member may appreciate, this was a course that was devised in order to have a useful role for our air squadrons, and I understand there is to be a sort of rotation between our squadrons in France and Germany so that they will be able to exercise both roles.
I do not believe I can add anything to what my colleague the Minister of National Defence has stated with regard to this matter both in the house and in the committee. I regret I cannot offhand give the cost of this particular move, but I will find out so that hon. members may have this information. I think the hon. member realizes that with regard to this matter of the air squadrons in Europe we are doing the best we can, having inherited a difficult situation.

subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO REMARK BY JUSTICE MINISTER
speechtext:
May I ask the hon. gentleman how there can be a possibility of rotating R.C.A.F. planes between France and Germany when our squadrons in Germany are equipped for the handling of nuclear weapons, whereas our squadrons in France are now being changed over to use only conventional weapons? Are all the planes to be changed so that they may fulfil a dual role?
20220-122J
Supply-National Defence

subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO REMARK BY JUSTICE MINISTER
speechtext: They are being changed, now, so that they will be able to carry out a dual role, and the pilots will also be rotated.

Mr. Chairman, I think I am allowed under this item to read a resolution passed by the district council of the Sague-nay-Lake St. John national labaur union.
We are considering today the administration of the Royal Canadian Air Force, and the resolution in question deals with the storage of nuclear arms at the Bagotville military base, which comes under the Royal Canadian Air Force, the expenditures of which we are now considering.
I will simply read the resolution:
At a regular meeting of the district council of the Saguenay-Lake St. John national labour union held at Arvida on January 19, 1964, a resolution was put forward asking the district council to protest strongly to the Prime Minister of Canada, and to the federal members of parliament of the district, against storage of nuclear warheads at the Bagotville base.
The council executive was directed to prepare the following resolution:
Considering the stand taken by the national labour union in previous conventions.
Considering the danger which such atomic weapons constitutes for the people of eur district in case of war.
Considering that the mere presence of such nuclear warheads on our soil makes our district a potential target and can transform this area into a radioactive desert.
Whereas such weapons do not constitute an effective means of long range defence.
Whereas Canada can play a doubly effective part by working for peace.
Our council asks the district, especially all representative bodies of our district, to protest to government authorities in order that they may abandon their projects.
We hope that you will take this letter under special consideration: your viewpoint would be very much appreciated by our members.
Yours truly,
Saguenay-Lake St. John Regional Local of the National Unions.
And it is signed Elmer Proulx, secretary.
Mr. Chairman, I want to be the mouth-piece of the national unions of the Saguenay-Lake St. John area and I strongly support this resolution on their part.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO REMARK BY JUSTICE MINISTER
speechtext:
Order. I allowed the hon. member to read the resolution he mentioned in order that we might determine its nature.
In my opinion, the question of nuclear weapons is not connected in any way, directly or indirectly, with the item under study; it even goes beyond the restricted limits of this item. Consequently, I invite the hon. member to restrict his observations to what he has just said.

subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO REMARK BY JUSTICE MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, please note that in credit 35e now under study, mention

Supply-National Defence is made of "miscellaneous materials and supplies, $1,150,000". Then, how can we say that in these miscellaneous supplies-nuclear weapons are also supplies, not only in winter but in fall and spring, they are miscellaneous supplies relating to airplanes at Bagotville?
I believe that these things, these supplies of fuel, gasoline, fuel oil, lubricants for aircraft and mechanical equipment, are related to the subject I am discussing now: supplies and upkeep of equipment. Supplementary estimates are being requested for the upkeep of that equipment at Bagotville, and I wish to say that I fully endorse the text of the resolution which has been approved unanimously by the labour union in my area and more especially in the Arvida-Jonquiere-Kenogami area.
The population, including the social and municipal bodies and the farmers' unions, object to the storage of nuclear arms in our area. But the government, here in Ottawa, refuses to recognize the objections raised by the whole population of one area.
Mr. Chairman, it becomes serious in my opinion when a government pays no attention and does not even care about the protests voiced by all the people, all the social and municipal bodies of an area, and keeps storing nuclear arms in a peaceful region inhabited by peace-minded citizens working peacefully and contributing to the development of our country.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO REMARK BY JUSTICE MINISTER
speechtext: I have listened with great interest to the remarks of the hon. member and I am sure he will agree with me that they are of a much too general a nature for the limited scope of the vote under consideration.

subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO REMARK BY JUSTICE MINISTER
speechtext:
Then, Mr. Chairman, I will conclude by speaking of this vote to which, I want to make it clear, I am opposed. It includes an amount of $1,150,000 for miscellaneous materials and supplies which will be used for the storage of nuclear weapons at Bagotville.
I wish to register a protest also against the vote for gasoline, fuel oil and lubricants for aircraft and mechanical equipment if that material is to be used for the storage of nuclear weapons.
I protest against this vote concerning repairs and maintenance of equipment, if this includes equipment to be used for storing nuclear arms at the Bagotville military base.
I protest, and I object to these estimates, not only in my own name, but on behalf of the whole population of the Saguenay-Lake St. John district. I do it with all the vigour I am capable of, and Mr. Chairman, when you ask if this item is agreed to, please


report that it is on division, and report further on division of the member for Lapointe.

subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO REMARK BY JUSTICE MINISTER
speechtext:
I should like to inquire what plans the department has for, or what the department intends to do with, the radar station in Edgar which is in my riding and which, I believe, will be closed as of July 1.
I should like to point out that this is a community of a certain size. It has its own fire brigade, its own power plant, three dormitories accommodating 500 people and about 85 housing units. The point I wish to make is that this is a responsibility of the federal government. An investment has been made amounting I believe to some $9 million. It has been accepted that the federal government has some role to play in education. For example, when vocational schools are constructed the federal government pays three quarters of the cost of the building and of the equipment used in the operation of those schools. I should like to go further and ask the minister what plans he has. Is he contemplating an educational centre or a vocational school, so that there may be continuity in this area?
I ask this because, as the minister knows, there is a choice between educating the people or making welfare payments, providing unemployment insurance, relief and so on. Therefore I say to him that while they are spending millions of dollars advising people to obtain more education so they will stay off the unemployment insurance and relief rolls, and so forth, on the other hand they cannot afford to close up a building such as this. I also want to stress the point that a great many workers have their roots in this community; they have been employed there for 11 or 12 years and have their homes in this area. Therefore I would appreciate an answer as to what the minister intends to do in this matter. I would state further that it is my opinion that some educational or semieducational plan should be adopted in order that those buildings can be utilized to the full, in view of the need today for further education.

subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO REMARK BY JUSTICE MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think my hon. friend should know that the department is certainly not indifferent to what is happening to some of these communities where the radar stations are being closed down. Having said how concerned we are with what is happening, I think it is only fair also to say that I believe it would not be logical policy for the department to keep maintaining and operating stations which are no longer useful.
What has been done and what is contemplated in the future is that whenever one of

these radar stations is to be disbanded, it is immediately turned over to crown assets. The Department of Defence Production and the Minister of Industry have in their own organization a group of people who are trying to establish contact with the provincial governments and other groups and associations to study how these radar stations might be usefully used. A real effort is being made in this sense in order to try and get the provinces interested in utilizing these very excellent facilities.
Another point, of course, is that most of these stations are in rather isolated areas, and it is difficult at times to interest people in going to these areas. However, Mr. Chairman, I can assure my hon. friend that everything it is humanly possible to do is now being done.

subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO REMARK BY JUSTICE MINISTER
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I want to thank the minister for his answer. I would draw to his attention that this is not a particularly isolated area; it is just about seven miles from a city one way and it is about 15 miles from a town with a population of 15,000. Also, it is only four miles off a super highway. I am wondering whether the minister, through dominion-provincial relations, could in some way get a program going of some form of education without even going through crown assets and wasting that time.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO REMARK BY JUSTICE MINISTER
speechtext: The hon. member for Edmonton West.

subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO REMARK BY JUSTICE MINISTER
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the hon member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm has asked me whether he might ask it first.

speechtext:
I should like to direct a question to the Associate Minister of National Defence. Does he intend to provide the College Militaire Royal de Saint Jean with a four year course, the same as Kingston?
Surely, the minister is aware that several of his colleagues from the province of Quebec, and particularly the Minister without Portfolio, the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis), have formally promised, on behalf of their party, that the College Militaire Royal de Saint Jean would have a four year course, the same as Kingston. That is why I am asking the minister whether or not that four year course will be established.

subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO REMARK BY JUSTICE MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the interest my hon. friend has always shown concerning this matter. Other hon. members from both sides of the house are also interested in it.
Now, for the Department of National Defence, it was not only a matter of reorganizing the armed forces, but reorganizing also
Supply-National Defence the military colleges. As I said before, we are carrying out a thorough study of military training with a view to revising it according to standards we consider necessary for our armed forces.
I regret no decision has yet been taken, and I am not in a position to give a definite answer to the hon. member's question.

subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO REMARK BY JUSTICE MINISTER
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I wish to ask a supplementary question. I asked the minister a very definite question, that is if the government would keep the promise made by some of its members, in particular the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napier-ville. I am not asking that it be kept within a month or two; whether it is at the end of this year or next year, I am asking the government if it will keep the distinct promise made on behalf of his party by the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville.

subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO REMARK BY JUSTICE MINISTER
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I would not like any misunderstanding about that. What I want to tell my hon. friend is that when the study I referred to is completed, we will take the most effective steps in the interest of the college and the country.

subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO REMARK BY JUSTICE MINISTER
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, with regard to the question asked by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon)-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO REMARK BY JUSTICE MINISTER
speechtext: Order. The hon. member for Edmonton West.

subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO REMARK BY JUSTICE MINISTER
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I should like to raise two points with the associate minister. First of all, from time to time in the past there has been some difficulty about travelling and moving expenses with regard to the air force, the army and the navy. I think the minister will agree that within the last year or so criminal charges have been laid with regard to the falsification of moving expenses. There have been some irregularities in this connection. I am wondering, therefore, what steps have been taken recently to eliminate as much as possible the giving of kickbacks and the other irregular practices which have cropped up from time to time. I do not say that they have existed only in recent years, but they have occurred from time to time. I remember that when I was associated with the Department of National Defence back in 1957, this was a problem. It has exercised the Canadian warehousemen's association, and they themselves very much deprecate the existence of these practices. There is somehow built into the present system of the movement of service personnel a type of facility which leads to these practices. I believe this is caused by the

Supply-National Defence competition. I do not know whether the Department of National Defence has worked out some arrangement with the Canadian warehousemen's association of policing this sort of thing. I know it is deprecated by service officers and certainly by the association as a whole.
However, we do know that such practices have existed and certainly excessive weights have been used at times. This has been drawn to the attention of the public by the Auditor General. I should like to receive an indication from the minister, either today or on some other occasion, as to just what has been done in order to tidy this up, so there is as little chance as possible for, shall we say, sharp practices in regard to moving expenses.
The other point I wish to raise with the hon. minister is this. Can he tell us at this stage-and there may be reasons why he cannot-what is to be the ultimate use of the four very large installations that were used by the United States air force as refuelling bases?
The last of these, Namao R.C.A.F. station, is to be phased out on July _1 next. There are some very extensive facilities. Some of the runways are used jointly with the R.C.A.F. and there are other buildings and what have you, such as fuel storage facilities, put up at the expense of the United States government, of which I am sure some very adequate use could be made, particularly at the two bases at Cold Lake and Namao.

subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO REMARK BY JUSTICE MINISTER
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, personally I have not been aware that there is any great wave of irregularities in connection with removal and travelling expenses. There are some recommendations contained in the Glassco commission report in this regard, but unfortunately I am not in a position to advise my hon. friend today what measures will be taken to correct the situation. However, I will look at the matter and inform him at a later date.

subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO REMARK BY JUSTICE MINISTER
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I wish to correct any misapprehension there may be. I am not saying there has been a great wave, but there have been cases. Individual members of the Canadian warehousemen's association have definitely spoken of this, and I would like to know what efforts are being made to control this sort of thing.

subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO REMARK BY JUSTICE MINISTER
speechtext: I will look into the matter.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO REMARK BY JUSTICE MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sorry to detain the minister for external affairs, but when he makes a statement in this house I take a little time to think over what he has said and then I go back and examine the record to see whether or not what he has said is accurate. I am glad he is now

here to listen to my submission, because a little while ago he attempted to make the case that the subject of Canada's participation in the United Nations Cyprus force should not be discussed under these estimates because the estimates were tabled on March 6. This is accurate. His statement concerning our participation in the Cyprus expedition was not made until March 13, so it follows that the estimates which were tabled on March 6 could not possibly have anything in them which would pertain to the Cyprus expedition.
I would point out, Mr. Chairman, that the subject of the troubles in Cyprus was raised in this house on Monday, February 24, by the hon. member for Edmonton West. The Prime Minister replied to him in these words which appear at page 129 of Hansard:
There has been no additional request made of Canada for participation in any such force but, as the house knows, we have laid down certain conditions which we feel should be observed before Canada participates in a force of that kind.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO REMARK BY JUSTICE MINISTER
speechtext: That is right.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO REMARK BY JUSTICE MINISTER
speechtext: Obviously the government was considering the question of Canada's participation in an international force as early as February 24.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO REMARK BY JUSTICE MINISTER
speechtext: Long before that.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO REMARK BY JUSTICE MINISTER
speechtext: When the Prime Minister and the minister of external affairs rose this afternoon to object to the hon. member for Oxford making a statement about the Cyprus expedition I knew that perhaps they were attempting to conceal something.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO REMARK BY JUSTICE MINISTER
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, my hon. friend has not helped his case by his last reference. There has never been any refusal to discuss this matter. Indeed, my hon. friend is now proving that we have had very considerable discussion. There is only one point before the committee at the present time and that is whether or not the particular item involves an expense which could be properly attributable to Canada's undertaking in the United Nations peace keeping force. That is the issue and no other. The question of Cyprus has been discussed many times in this house, but what we are now concerned with is this particular item of expenditure. I would suggest, Mr. Chairman, that unless the hon. gentleman addresses himself to that point he is not in order.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO REMARK BY JUSTICE MINISTER
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, we can always expect an intervention by the minister of external affairs no matter which side of the house he sits on.

subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO REMARK BY JUSTICE MINISTER
speechtext: And against the rules too.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO REMARK BY JUSTICE MINISTER
speechtext: Yes, generally against the rules. I did not say that anything was being concealed. I said that perhaps there was an attempt at concealment. When the minister of external affairs is talking with that skill and verbosity which is his and his alone, there is sometimes the expectation on the part of some hon. members that there is concealment involved.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO REMARK BY JUSTICE MINISTER
speechtext: Be careful now.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO REMARK BY JUSTICE MINISTER
speechtext:
I am making no accusation. Yesterday I was asking him about regular forces from Greece and Turkey and he persisted in talking about Cypriot forces which I had not even mentioned; so the minister is sometimes not very clear in his activities.
I direct my attention specifically to the estimate in front of us, which is a vote of over $13 million, involving some $1.5 million for travelling and removal expenses, another item of $3.5 million for gasoline, fuel oil, and so on. It will take a little convincing to persuade me that these very large items are not related in some way to the expectation that Canada would participate in some overseas activity under United Nations command. Because as the minister for external affairs said when I mentioned February 24, the government was considering such a thing earlier than that. A government which boasted of its decision would surely have made plans prior to that with regard to the expenses for the air force and army. It might have interrupted the writing of the white paper by the Minister of National Defence; perhaps that was the delay which was caused. But I am sure he was figuring out how much more it would cost if Canada participated in a United Nations force. Consequently that is why I question the earlier intervention of the minister of external affairs in trying to persuade the house that nothing in these supplementary estimates pertain to that matter.

subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO REMARK BY JUSTICE MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make the suggestion that we go much further than giving up this hour. I see little value in giving up this private members' hour if it is going to do nothing to shorten this debate.
I do not think there is any reason to attribute blame for this. I think one should recognize that it has been a long time since members have had an ample opportunity to examine the various departments and to question the various ministers. There was a long time when there were no estimates. The general estimates for last session came in during the closing days of the session. Many members were willing to forgo questions they wanted to ask and matters they wanted to raise in the interests of winding up the session at a reasonable time. So I do not think that any real blame attaches to members for the fact that these supplementary estimates have taken a considerable period of time.
On the other hand, I think it is most advisable now to try to wind up the discussion of these supplementary estimates. It just means that discussion of the supplementary estimates may go on for another hour or for a stipulated period of time. If it is agreeable to the other parties in the house we would be prepared to give an undertaking to dispose of these

Supply-National Defence supplementary estimates not later than ten o'clock tomorrow night. If we finish sooner, so much the better, but we would be prepared to terminate any discussion by ten o'clock tomorrow evening.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I did not ask the minister to get up immediately. He might have let me finish my sentence. I wonder what his explanation will be. Perhaps he would like to give it now in view of the answer he gave half a minute ago.

I think it would perhaps save a lot of time if I were to take the different items and give an explanation of them. As far as the first item of $1,445,000 is concerned, the explanation is that which was given by the President of the Privy Council. It has to do with the removal and travelling of personnel. The average cost per move had been estimated too low at $120 per move and had to be increased to $147. There was additional cost in regard to transfers brought about by the withdrawal of the CF-100 squadrons from Europe late in 1962 and 1963 and the disbanding of No. 426 squadron and other units for which many claims and accounts were not paid until 1963 and early in 1964. Then another factor is the price increase for packing, crating and transportation put into effect by the Canadian warehousemen's association, and that accounts for this amount of $1,445,000.
In so far as materials and supplies are concerned, there is fuel for heating and cooking. The forecast was over-expended by $305,000 and this was mainly due to an underestimate for the 18 new radar units introduced into the R.C.A.F. in 1962-63.
Did the minister mention radar equipment?
Yes, 18 new radar units introduced into the air force.
Where is that used; I wonder if the minister can tell us?

I understand that these were taken over when we had a change-over of administration between the United States and Canada on the Pine Tree line.
Then, there is the item for gasoline, fuel oil and lubricants for aircraft. There has been historically a shortfall in the annual flying
Supply-National Defence hours which logistic staffs have usually applied to estimates for oils and lubricants of 15 per cent. However, the 1962-63 totals were not available when the 1963-64 estimates were prepared. So far this year indications have been that the shortfall will be very small this year.

On that point, I wonder if the minister could assure the committee that none of the $3.5 million used for the purchase of these aircraft lubricants was used for lubricants or fuel for aircraft going to Cyprus in this operation?
Because of the time involved, I would be morally certain that it did not. These estimates, of course, were made before we were involved in this operation.

Just on that point, Mr. Chairman, may I say that I thought when we were having a few words with the minister of external affairs on this point, the understanding was that away back in February the armed services were preparing for the Cyprus operation. One branch of the armed services is the air force and one purpose of the air force is transport. I should like to know, and I am sure other hon. members would like to know, if any of these $3.5 million worth of gasoline and lubricants were used in these aircraft transporting Canadian personnel to Cyprus, or by aircraft on the island of Cyprus.
The minister would have to be very certain before he answered that question because $3.5 million is a lot of money. As has been pointed out before, these supplementary estimates (E) are the fifth supplementary estimates and are the final ones for the year. Surely the Minister of National Defence, the minister looking after these estimates and the Secretary of State for External Affairs have looked into these matters and will have looked into them as far back as Christmas time when the Cyprus operation or some other necessary peace keeping operation for which Canada would have to be prepared was in their minds. I said the minister would have to be careful in answering. Were there, to his knowledge, any of the oils or lubricants accounted for by this item used in transporting Canadian personnel to Cyprus?

I am quite sure that the
members of the house want to get ahead with the work of the committee and want to see this matter pushed through as quickly as possible. I have stated that I am personally sure there is not any amount of money involved in these items that was used in the transport to Cyprus. I am informed that the bills for that particular exercise have

Supply-National Defence not been received as yet. I am morally certain that there is nothing for the Cyprus exercise that is reflected in these items.

The minister is saying, then, that up until the final decision to go to Cyprus, which was after these estimates were prepared, the Royal Canadian Air Force was not prepared in any way, shape or form. None of these lubricants were used in these aircraft or in any of the aircraft which would have been used in Cyprus. It seems ridiculous to me to think that there was no preparation. Surely, there was preparation. The Secretary of State for External Affairs said that it was well before February when preparations were made. Surely there was a state of preparedness on the part of the Royal Canadian Air Force and the other armed services in Canada which would involve these expnditures being made. We have heard that we have not had the bills for Cyprus, but have we had the bills for the preparations and are they part of these supplementary estimates?

The main factors in the increase in the 1962-63 accounts carried forward for this year include underestimate for liquid and gaseous oxygen for new aircraft, Yukon CF-101 and CF-104; underestimate for chemicals related to increased requirements mainly for water purification chemicals for new radar sites; underestimate for miscellaneous cordate and textiles; new requirement for hexafluoride gas for FPS 26 and 27 radars.

The last item, $1,239,000 includes underestimation for non-residential school fees and school contributions. This completes the amount of $13,653,000 which I feel has nothing whatever to do with the operation in Cyprus.

Mr. Chairman, a few minutes ago, I was listening to the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) discuss the course given at the College Mili-taire Royal de Saint Jean, and ask the minister for an extension of two years, as it is the case for the Kingston Royal Military College. That is a bit more than a fervent wish, but you can take it anyway you like.
In any case, how could he make such a promise, when the government was merely wishing. Could it be that the Minister without Portfolio exceeded his rights in making that promise or that some responsible member of his party had told him that the thing was coming, in short, that it was one of the government's projects?
Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member has as much experience in politics as I have, and there is no need for me to answer that question.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The hon. member may not see the relevance of the argument. It is simply this. We cannot get the answers to questions from the government. If they would give us the answers, we would move on to the next problem. I asked the Associate Minister of National Defence certain questions with regard to the air force in Europe-this is the item of the estimates that pertains to the matter- and he cannot give me the answers.
May I ask him another question. He told us earlier that the aircraft in Europe are to be modified so they can carry nuclear weapons as well as conventional weapons. Let him now tell us how many have been so modified and what is the cost per plane for that modification.
Mr. Chairman, I answered that question a while ago and said I did not know how much it would cost.

speechtext:

Mr. Chairman-

Will you let me speak.
Now, when I was sitting on the other side of the house, I always requested that consideration be given to the feasibility of giving a complete course-

Mr. Chairman, on a point of order. The minister should not question the word of an hon. member. He questions what was said by the hon. member for Megantic (Mr. Langlois), and what I stated myself. We maintain that the minister-
That is not a point of order.
-gave a solemn promise-
A private member, or a single member, like the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm has no right to question the word of a minister, and more particularly not what I said.
I challenge your point of order.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman. I do not know what the minister is referring to, although he has questioned, as the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm has said, the word of some hon. members and mine.
These are exactly the words I said earlier: if the minister made a solemn promise to his voters-
Mr. Chairman-

Let me finish. The Associate Minister of National Defence answered that the question of extending the course at the College Militaire Royal de Saint Jean by two years had not been decided yet. If the minister did make this formal promise, I reiterate my earlier statement, that he lied to his voters.

To sum up the discussion, I never promised that there would be an additional course, but I promised that, as soon as the Liberal government came to power, consideration would be given to the advisability of a full course. I have proof here in my hand. I know that the hon. member for Megantic is quite sincere. I wonder whether
Supply-National Defence the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm is; I am wondering.
I promised my constituents to look after the matter, as opposed to what the Conservatives were doing when they were sitting on this side of the house. They fooled around for six years and did nothing for the College Militaire Royal de Saint Jean, while I urged them to do something.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. If the minister wishes to correct the statements which may have been made concerning him, let him do it while remaining within the scope of the present debate.

May I say, Mr. Chairman, that my remarks will not go beyond the scope of the debate.
When I was sitting in the opposition I requested from the then minister of national defence that the advisability of giving a complete course at the College Militaire Royal de Saint Jean be considered.
Now, on the 4th of November, the Minister of National Defence answered a letter of mine in which I had previously requested-
In what year?

-and here is my request to him.
I shall give you all that, because it is interesting for the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, and to prove to him that we are looking after the interests of the voters, in accordance with what we say to them, during an election campaign.
On November 18, 1963, I wrote to the Minister of National Defence-and I would like the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm to listen, because he would learn a few things:

My dear Paul:
Thanks to the Liberal party, we have in Saint Jean, P.Q., a bilingual royal military college. However, as you know, this college dispenses only the first years of the course that has to be completed in Kingston. This situation is unfortunate and abnormal.

As you can see, my attitude has not changed since I have been sitting on this side of the house.
Convince your colleagues first.

Listen to me. I shall continue: [Text]
We believe that the College Militaire Royal in Saint Jean should be organized in order to dispense the complete course, starting next September.
During the years when the Conservative party was in power, I made many interventions about this in the House of Commons. Your predecessors:

Supply-National Defence
General Pearkes, Colonel Harkness and Pierre Se-vigny, answered that they were giving serious consideration to this question... but nothing was done.
I do not believe that since I am sitting with the government, I should refrain from asking for a complete course at the College Militaire Royal de St. Jean.
As Minister of National Defence, you are the president of the C.M.R., and as such, I am sure, that you will be proud to give instructions in order to permit this college to give a complete course. Could you tell me what has been done up to now by your department in view of permitting such a course?
As the C.M.R. has been established by our party,
I think that it is imperative for our Liberal government to complete that great achievement. Why should we wait any longer to take a decision when we all know that this has to be done one day?
Hoping to receive encouraging words from you very soon, I remain

Subsequent to Lucien Cardin's appointment as associate minister-
-and the minister is here tonight-
-he asked for a full report concerning the establishment of third and fourth years at College Militaire Royal de Saint Jean. This report is now being studied as part of my review of defence matters, and I should hope to be in a position soon to let you know the department's decision concerning the proposal that the third and fourth years be provided at College Militaire Royal de Saint Jean.

I protest when the hon. member tor Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm attempts, as usual, to cast doubts on my interest in my constituents and the fair claims of the province of Quebec. The hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm may well laugh, but during the six years when his government was in office he did nothing for the College Militaire Royal de Saint Jean. But I did write to my government and I continue to make the same demands as when I was in opposition.
I do not think it is very intelligent on the part of the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm to try to delay the debate-
Keep quiet.

-try and delay the passing of the estimates. You want me to stop talking. But you, yourself, are asking me questions and when you get the answers, you want me to stop talking. I want you to know that I will not. You are insolent in your remarks and you make claims which are totally inaccurate.
Mr. Chairman, I wanted very much to put the record straight to let the house, the riding of St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville as

well as the whole province of Quebec know that when you belong to the Liberal party, whether you sit on one side of the house or the other, you keep on doing your work honestly. When in office, we still ask for the same things we did while in opposition, whereas some people, the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm for instance, kneel before their leader, the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) without asking for anything for Quebec during the six years their party was in power.

Mr. Chairman, on this side of the house we intended to vote these estimates before six o'clock, but since the minister does not want to co-operate with the ministers of his own party, we shall not be able to do so.
Mr. Chairman, to show the extent to which the Minister without Portfolio lacks judgment, he has written a letter in English to the Minister of National Defence instead of writing to the Associate Minister of National Defence who resides in the province of Quebec.
